results.title: المشروبات المحلاة والوجبات السريعة.. مخاطر تهدد الكبد
results.description: حذّرت المديرة التنفيذية لمركز بحوث «التغذية الصحية» الدكتورة نوريا ديانوفا، من الإفراط في تناول الأطعمة والمشروبات الغنية بالسكريات والدهون، لما قد تسببه من مشكلات صحية تؤثر في الكبد، مؤكدةً أن الاعتقاد بضرورة تنظيف الكبد بصورةٍ دوريةٍ للتخلص من السموم مجردُ خرافةٍ، إذ يمتلك الكبد القدرة على أداء هذه الوظيفة بصورةٍ طبيعيةٍ.وأوضحت أن الخطر الأكبر على صحة الكبد لا يكمن في نوعية الأطعمة وحدها، وإنما في الإفراط في استهلاكها، مشيرةً إلى أن تناول سعرات حرارية تفوق حاجات الجسم يسهم في الإصابة بالسمنة ومقاومة الأنسولين، ويزيد احتمالات الإصابة بأمراض الكبد.وبيّنت أن المشروبات الكحولية تُعد من أبرز المواد الضارة بالكبد، نتيجة تأثيراتها السامة في خلاياه، إلى جانب أضرارها على الدماغ والقلب، فضلاً عن دورها في تعزيز تراكم الدهون داخل خلايا الكبد، ما قد يؤدي إلى الإصابة بالكبد الدهني المرتبط بالكحول، مؤكدةً أن تناول الكحول ينطوي على مخاطرَ صحيةٍ حتى عند استهلاك كمياتٍ قليلةٍ.وحذّرت من الإفراط في استهلاك المشروبات الغازية المحلاة والعصائر المعبأة والشاي المثلج المحلى ومشروبات القهوة المضاف إليها الشراب السكري، واصفةً إياها بأنها «قنابل استقلابية»، لما تحتويه من كمياتٍ مرتفعةٍ من السكريات التي قد تسهم في اضطرابات التمثيل الغذائي وتراكم الدهون في الكبد.ودعت إلى الحد من تناول الوجبات السريعة والكربوهيدرات المكررة والأطعمة الغنية بالدهون المتحولة والمشبعة، واستبدالها بمصادرَ غذائيةٍ أكثرَ فائدةً، تشمل البروتينات النباتية والأسماك والبقوليات.وأكدت أن حماية الكبد من الأمراض لا تتطلب اللجوء إلى برامج إزالة السموم أو ما يُعرف بتنظيف الكبد، وإنما تعتمد على اتباع نظامٍ غذائيٍ صحيٍ ومتوازنٍ، يرتكز على تنوع الأغذية النباتية الغنية بالألياف، وتجنب الإفراط في تناول السعرات الحرارية.
creator: عكاظ (جدة)

results.title: Inheritance: The Long March of the New Era
results.description: BEIJING, Oct. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- An interview from China.org.cn with Wang Xiaohui and David Ferguson on the Long March: Inheritance: The Long March of the New Era Wang Xiaohui: The Long March went on for two years. The Red Army trekked 25,000 li across some of China's harshest terrain, but they kept their heads high, seeking hope amid despair and marching towards light through unending darkness. Do you think the Long March has ended? Why are people still talking about it 90 years later? David Ferguson: China's history records that the reunion of the three main forces of the Red Army at Huining and Jiangtaibu brought an end to the Long March. If you see the Long March purely as a military campaign, then yes, it did end there. But if you see the Long March as a spirit, then it has never truly come to an end. We often speak of the "new Long March" today. What began as a simple metaphor has grown into a faithful portrait of how Long March spirit echoes through every facet of contemporary China. Here I have some stories to illustrate this. "If we can make this work, I believe the Party will judge us based on facts." On a chilly night in 1978, Yan Hongchang, deputy head of the Xiaogang Village production team, said this to his fellow villagers. That night, Yan and 17 other farmers huddled inside an earth farmhouse and pressed their fingerprints on a secret contract to divide collective farmland among individual households. At that time, the act carried immense risks, and no one could foresee the consequences it would bring. The following year, they each harvested enough to sustain a household for five years, ending more than two decades of reliance on reliefs. The household contract responsibility system proved a resounding success. The spark ignited in Xiaogang Village soon blazed into a nationwide rural reform campaign. In 1982, the CPC Central Committee issued the first "No. 1 Central Document" on rural work, clarifying that the household contract responsibility system was a legitimate system under socialist collective economy, a framework that endures to this day. Around the same time as Xiaogang's bold experiment, a blast broke ground at Shekou, Shenzhen — the construction of the China Merchants Shekou Industrial Zone kicked off, sounding the opening salvo of China's reform and opening up drive. Yuan Geng, the zone's director who was already in his sixties, erected a sign bearing the slogan "Time is money, efficiency is life," which sparked heated controversy at the time. Yet the sign was never replaced, standing witness to countless bold, once-unimaginable reforms taking shape. Shenzhen grew into a pioneer of experimental reforms, and the special economic zones delivered miracles of economic take-off. China has developed rapidly in the decades since reform and opening up. Rural residents had enough to eat and keep warm, and the countryside became a rock-solid guarantee for the whole country's food security, while agricultural modernization advanced by leaps and bounds. Supported by robust agricultural development, China completed an industrialization journey in mere decades that took Western developed countries centuries, yielding universally recognized social and economic achievements. A secret pact and a groundbreaking blast wrote the opening chapter of China's modern development. Tracing back to their spiritual roots, every milestone along this magnificent journey rests on the same truth-seeking spirit forged by the CPC during the Long March. On June 23, 2020, the serenity over Xichang in southwestern China's Sichuan Province was shattered by a thunderous roar. A Long March-3B carrier rocket soared aloft in blazing flames, lifting the 55th and final satellite of the BeiDou-3 Navigation Satellite System into orbit. All of China's carrier rockets bear the unified name "Long March." Decades ago, Red Army soldiers wearing straw sandals crossed snow-capped mountains and marshlands on a life-or-death journey that shaped the fate of the Chinese nation. Today, China's aerospace trailblazers carry the "Long March" banner into the boundless cosmos, embarking on another expedition. The core spirit of confronting hardships head-on and refusing to surrender has resonated from earth to space. The BeiDou Navigation System secured China its own place on the world's navigation map; Chang'e-6 has extended humanity's reach to the far side of the Moon; the C919, China's homegrown large passenger aircraft, soars into the skies; breakthroughs keep emerging in cutting-edge fields such as artificial intelligence and quantum technology. On this new Long March, China surmounts obstacles and new frontiers of innovation — just as the Red Army once pressed forward unflinchingly against overwhelming odds to claim victory on the Long March. Having blazed its own unique path of development, China also shares the development wisdom and spiritual strength forged on the Long March with the wider world. Outcomes under the Global Development Initiative bear tangible fruit: From civilian water wells and cross-border railways across Africa to Luban Workshops that provide vocational training in many countries around the world, China adheres to the philosophy of "teaching others how to fish," letting the partner nations take the initiative to independently pursue growth paths suited to their national realities. Taking lead in acting on the Global Security Initiative, China is the largest contributor of UN peacekeeping personnel among all permanent members of the UN Security Council, protecting civilians in the conflict zones worldwide. The Global Civilization Initiative dismantles the biased "clash of civilizations" rhetoric, encouraging civilizations to nourish one another through communication and mutual learning. The Global Governance Initiative advocates a simple yet important principle: Global affairs should be discussed and handled through broad consultation. Standing firmly on the right side of history, China has worked to steer global governance towards a fairer and more equitable order. These four global initiatives are vivid practice of the Communist Party of China's vision of building a shared future with the world, and a contemporary extension of the Long March spirit. China never imposes its own development models on others; it only upholds down-to-earth exploration tailored to local realities. China rejects zero-sum calculations in favor of cooperation based on goodwill and shared progress. Through its own development, the country brings benefits to the rest of the world, honoring its founding aspiration to advance human progress and build a better future for all. These stories make me think. In a socialist country like China, how do you develop a market economy? How do you achieve reform and opening up? In a country as vast and complex as China, how do you raise every single individual out of absolute poverty? In the face of technological pain points and the challenges of development, how do you find a way forward? On a global scale, how do we confront the challenges facing all of humanity? In a way, these questions are no different to the questions faced by the Red Army on the Long March. There were no ready-made answers then and there are no ready-made answers now. Under the leadership of the CPC, China is in the process of finding its answers to these questions. And in so doing, it has embarked on a new Long March for a new era. This new Long March was never a journey taken in isolation. As China carved out its own development path, the faith and fortitude tempered amid snow peaks and marshlands have crossed national borders, delivering Chinese insights into coping with the shared challenges facing humanity. Only those who embrace the world can truly go the distance. Born from a trek of 25,000 li, the spirit of the Long March is no longer merely China's spiritual treasure — it also speaks to a universal pursuit — humanity's courage to seek truth, overcome adversity, and advance together in solidarity. China Mosaic http://www.china.org.cn/video/node_7230027.htm http://www.china.org.cn/2026-10/21/content_118743527.shtml

results.title: Trump's green card curbs test Indian tech workers' American dream
results.description: MUMBAI — The United States has long been a preferred destination for millions of Indian engineers, scientists and technology professionals seeking prospective career and permanent residency. However, the Trump administration’s decision to suspend the participation of several major technology companies in the Permanent Labour Certification Program, or PERM, has created fresh uncertainty for Indian workers aspiring to settle in the country. Earlier this month, the US announced it would suspend eight technology firms, including Microsoft, India's Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro and HCL Technologies, from hiring skilled international workers on a permanent basis through a widely used visa pathway, according to BBC.New and pending applications under PERM have been frozen. This is a big blow to Indians who hold a majority of H-1B visas — a temporary visa for specialists — which they used to work in the US while relying on PERM to get a green card and, ultimately, citizenship. The latest announcement is in line with Trump's push for stricter skilled-worker immigration rules, which tech firms have been adapting to and, therefore, the impact on businesses may be minimal, experts say. Nasscom, the trade association of India's $300 billion technology industry, says that Indian companies have reduced the dependence on H-1B visas and are hiring more locally."Consequently, the number of employees transitioning from H-1B visas to permanent residency through the PERM process is also relatively limited," the association adds. Wipro said in a statement that more than 80% of its workforce in the US is locally hired. Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) said its PERM applications were in single digits in the last two years. Microsoft said in a statement that it has filed for H-1B visas mostly to retain existing staff, not to import new workers. A report in Business Standard newspaper, citing PERM Tracker, said, TCS' applications filings fell to two in 2025-26 from 513 in the previous year and 1,804 in the year before that. The report said no records were found for Infosys and Wipro for 2025-26.BBC's email to all eight companies asking questions about the impact of the restriction and how they were supporting affected employees in the US remained unanswered. Brokerage firm HDFC Securities said the impact on tech firms would be minimal, as PERM-linked jobs make up only a small share of revenue, even if higher-paid American workers replace them. But the US government's decision has an impact beyond business. A US-based senior executive with one of these eight firms told the BBC on condition of anonymity that the new PERM restriction will "not break the business", but the impact is more "intense" at a human level."A good number of people we know are stuck in a space where they have spent some years in the US but their green card application hasn't moved. Even if they are ready to move back to India, their children don't want to because they grew up here," he said. Recent policy moves have deepened uncertainty and amplified online hostility towards Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders. Researchers at Stop AAPI Hate, a US non-profit that combats anti-Asian and Pacific Islander discrimination, have reported a sharp increase in anti-South Asian online sentiment since the 2024 US election, with Indian immigrants and H-1B visa holders being frequent targets. While barring the eight tech companies from PERM, US Vice President JD Vance too referred to foreign professionals holding H-1B visas as "foreign indentured servants".While he later acknowledged that it was an "imperfect" rhetoric, his remark drew sharp criticism from India's foreign ministry which called it "unwarranted" and "deeply offensive" for the colonial connotation. Poorvi Chothani, founder and managing partner of global immigration law firm LawQuest, said many came to the US for better prospects, borrowing heavily to study and build careers. But as rules tighten now, they have fewer options and less ability to absorb the costs. Immigration experts believe that as pathways for residency become limited, some may reconsider their future in the US, while others may choose not to move at all. Ahmet Gulek, Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford's Immigration Policy Lab, told BBC that despite alternate ways to get residency, not many may be feasible. While moving to another firm not covered by the suspension is an option, he flags that it's unclear if those firms would be open to hiring immigrants given "the fear of retaliation".Besides, it's also a tough time to change jobs. The technology industry has already been reshaped by layoffs, cost-cutting and the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI), making career moves tougher. But there are other routes to a US green card. People with exceptional accomplishments or whose work advances national interests may be eligible for categories that bypass the PERM labour certification process. Applicants can also qualify for permanent residency by investing at least $800,000 in eligible US enterprises. Gulek warns some of these categories "may be targeted next."While Chothani says some are so keen to stay in the US that they are considering the EB-5 investor route but may not have enough capital to invest. Nearly one million Indian nationals were waiting for employment-based green cards as of December 2025, representing 79% of the total pending applications, according to the National Foundation for American Policy (NFAP).Their report projects wait times ranging from five to 179 years for highly skilled Indians filing labour certification or employment-based immigration petitions from January 2026, depending on the visa category. Like other recent immigration measures, the PERM suspension may face federal court challenges. But together, these moves signal a more restrictive climate for those hoping to study, work or settle in the US.Earlier, the Trump administration imposed a $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B visa petitions, a measure that was later struck down by federal courts. More recently, it has also proposed a $70,000 fee for universities recommending international students for a programme that allows graduates to work in the country after completing their studies."This trend is not changing anytime soon," said an Indian professional, who spoke to BBC on condition of anonymity and has transitioned to an H-1B visa recently after a "long wait". He says both the Republican Party and the Democratic Party agree immigration laws need reform, even if they disagree on how. Some research suggests that restrictions could shift jobs to India rather than to American workers. This is supported by industry players saying that they are already witnessing an increase in companies offshoring work."Companies benefit from cost arbitrage when they move work offshore. Post Covid, there is also greater acceptance and appreciation for remote work from clients," the executive from the tech firm earlier quoted says. Experts believe America's appetite for Indian tech talent is unlikely to disappear. What may be changing is how it taps that talent. For Indian professionals, that could mean rewriting the script about building a future in the US.
creator: agencies
